full_text:
यूपी में कैसा रहेगा मौसम? तापमान में गिरावट से कई जिलों में बढ़ेगी ठंड, मौसम विभाग ने जारी किया अपडेट
उत्तर प्रदेश में सुबह-शाम ठंड जारी है और दिन में धूप निकल रही है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, आने वाले दिनों में तापमान में गिरावट से ठंड बढ़ेगी।
HighLights
सुबह-शाम ठंड जारी, दिन में धूप निकल रही है।
आने वाले दिनों में तापमान में और गिरावट संभव।
28 अक्टूबर को पूर्वी यूपी में हल्की बारिश के आसार।
डिजिटल डेस्क, लखनऊ। उत्तर प्रदेश के कई हिस्सों में सुबह-शाम ठंड का दौर जारी है। वहीं, दिन में धूप निकल रही है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, आने वाले दिनों में मौसम को कोई बड़ा बदलाव देखने को नहीं मिल सकता है। प्रदेश के अधिकांश हिस्सों में मौसम शुष्क रहने की बात कही गई है।
IMD के अनुसार, प्रदेश के पूर्वी और पश्चिमी हिस्से में आने वाले दिनों में मौसम शुष्क रहने की संभावना है। इसके साथ ही, सुबह-शाम ठंड में बढ़ने के भी आसार हैं। 28 अक्टूबर को कई इलाकों में छिटपुट बारिश हो सकती है।
यूपी में मौसम का हाल
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 22 अक्टूबर से 27 अक्टूबर तक प्रदेश के पूर्वी और पश्चिमी हिस्से में मौसम शुष्क रहने की संभावना है। हालांकि, 28 अक्टूबर को पूर्वी यूपी के कुछ इलाकों में हल्की बारिश या बूंदाबांदी हो सकती है।
शांत हवाओं के बीच नमी में बढ़ोतरी
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार अधिकांश जिलों में हवा की गति शांत रही। हवा में उच्च आद्रता के कारण सुबह के समय दृश्यता पर हल्का असर पड़ सकता है। आने वाले दिनों में पश्चिमी विक्षोभ और उत्तर-पश्चिमी हवाओं के प्रभाव से न्यूनतम तापमान में और गिरावट आने की संभावना व्यक्त की जा रही है, जिससे ठंड का असर और बढ़ सकता है।

24 और 25 को पहाड़ों पर बारिश के आसार, चंडीगढ़ समेत ट्राईसिटी में बढ़ेगी ठंड; बच्चों-बुजुर्गों में वायरल का डर
पहाड़ों पर बारिश की संभावना के बीच चंडीगढ़ ट्राईसिटी में ठंड बढ़ने के आसार हैं। बदलते मौसम के कारण बच्चों ...और पढ़ें
HighLights
रात का तापमान करीब 15 डिग्री दर्ज किया जा रहा।
दिन का तापमान 29 से 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच।
मौसम में बदलाव के कारण स्वास्थ्य सावधानी बरतें।
जागरण संवाददाता, चंडीगढ़। पहाड़ों में बारिश की संभावना के बीच चंडीगढ़ ट्राईसिटी में ठंड बढ़ने के आसार हैं। मौसम विभाग के पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार, 24 और 25 अक्टूबर को हिमाचल प्रदेश के कुछ हिस्सों में बारिश हो सकती है।
पंजाब और हरियाणा के भी कुछ इलाकों में हल्की बारिश होने की संभावना है। पश्चिमी विक्षोभ के प्रभाव से मौसम में बदलाव देखने को मिल सकता है। बारिश के बाद तापमान में गिरावट आने से सुबह और शाम के समय ठंड का अहसास बढ़ सकता है।
चंडीगढ़, मोहाली और पंचकूला में फिलहाल भारी बारिश का अलर्ट नहीं है, लेकिन पड़ोसी राज्यों में मौसम बदलने का असर ट्राईसिटी के तापमान पर भी पड़ सकता है। मौसम में बदलाव की वजह से बच्चों और बुजुर्गों में वायरल का खतरा रहेगा।
इन दिनों शहर में रात का तापमान करीब 15 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज किया जा रहा है, जबकि दिन का तापमान 29 से 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच बना हुआ है। दिन में तेज धूप के कारण गर्मी महसूस होती है, वहीं रात में तापमान गिरने से ठंड बढ़ जाती है।
दिन और रात के तापमान में अंतर के कारण लोगों को सुबह और देर शाम ठंड का सामना करना पड़ रहा है। मौसम में होने वाले इस बदलाव के बीच स्वास्थ्य के प्रति सतर्क रहने की जरूरत है।
बदलते मौसम के बीच अस्पतालों में वायरल संक्रमण से जुड़ी शिकायतें भी देखने को मिल रही हैं। सर्दी-जुकाम, खांसी, गले में खराश और बुखार जैसे लक्षणों को लेकर लोग चिकित्सकों से परामर्श ले रहे हैं।
ऐसे मौसम में बच्चों, बुजुर्गों और पहले से बीमार लोगों को विशेष सावधानी बरतने की जरूरत है। चिकित्सकों की सलाह है कि मौसम के अनुसार कपड़े पहनें, ठंड से बचें और पर्याप्त पानी पीते रहें। लगातार बुखार, सांस लेने में परेशानी या अन्य गंभीर लक्षण होने पर चिकित्सकीय सलाह लें।

full_text:
[वीडियो] आज रात और कल, 23 अक्टूबर, 2026 के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान: मध्य और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में गरज के साथ बारिश कम होगी, उत्तरी वियतनाम में तापमान बढ़ेगा।
देश भर में मौसम शुष्क होता जा रहा है क्योंकि बारिश लाने वाले मौसम तंत्र कमजोर पड़ रहे हैं। उत्तर में, कुछ क्षेत्रों में सुबह-सुबह कोहरा छाएगा, जिसके बाद दिन में धूप खिली रहेगी। मध्य, मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी क्षेत्रों में, गरज के साथ बारिश धीरे-धीरे कम होगी और धूप निकलेगी; हालांकि, कुछ क्षेत्रों में बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवाओं का खतरा बना रहेगा।
उत्तरी वियतनाम में ठंडी हवा का एक कमजोर झोंका पूर्व की ओर बढ़ता जा रहा है, इसलिए मौसम अपेक्षाकृत स्थिर बना हुआ है। रात के दौरान, उत्तर-पश्चिम और उत्तर-पूर्व क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ बौछारें पड़ेंगी, जो तटीय प्रांतों में अधिक केंद्रित होंगी। सुबह तड़के, कुछ क्षेत्रों में कोहरा रहेगा और उत्तर-पश्चिम में ठंडक रहेगी। 23 अक्टूबर को, दोनों क्षेत्रों में धूप खिली रहेगी और बारिश केवल कुछ स्थानों पर ही होगी, मुख्य रूप से तटीय प्रांतों में दोपहर और शाम के समय।
थान्ह होआ और हा तिन्ह प्रांतों में ठंडी हवा का प्रभाव धीरे-धीरे कम हो रहा है, जिससे बारिश कम हो रही है और केवल कुछ स्थानों पर ही रात में बारिश होगी। दिन के समय मौसम शुष्क और धूप वाला रहेगा।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
क्वांग त्रि - ह्यू और दक्षिण मध्य तट पर, उत्तर से आने वाली ठंडी हवा और पूर्वी हवा क्षेत्र में उत्पन्न गड़बड़ी कमजोर पड़ रही है। रात में कुछ ही स्थानों पर हल्की बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आएगा, जो ज्यादा देर तक नहीं चलेगा। अगले दिन, पूरे क्षेत्र में मौसम आमतौर पर शुष्क और धूप वाला रहेगा।
मध्य उच्चभूमि और दक्षिणी वियतनाम में निम्न दबाव का क्षेत्र कमजोर हो रहा है और पूर्वी हवाएँ भी धीमी हैं, इसलिए गरज के साथ बारिश की संभावना कम रहेगी। रात के दौरान दोनों क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश होगी। 23 अक्टूबर को मौसम धूप वाला रहेगा और दोपहर और शाम के समय कुछ ही स्थानों पर गरज के साथ बारिश होगी।
हालांकि मौसम आमतौर पर अधिक अनुकूल है, फिर भी लोगों को उन क्षेत्रों में बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवाओं के झोंकों से सावधान रहने की जरूरत है जहां गरज के साथ तूफान आते हैं।

full_text:
Asia to face extreme heat, droughts, floods as unprecedented El Niño looms: UN
The global agency also said that some 50 million people could face increased hunger because of the weather phenomenon
The current El Niño event could be unprecedented in strength, and will peak towards the end of 2026 but its impacts will be felt long after that, with possible “shocks for the global economy” and hit Asia and other regions in the Global South with droughts, floods and extreme heat, the United Nations has said.
According to the latest Global Seasonal Climate Update from World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific – the epicentre of the extreme El Niño weather phenomenon – may rise to 3.8℃ above average between November 2026 and January 2027.
“We are already witnessing extreme weather events and expect this to multiply and cascade as El Niño intensifies,” Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of WMO said.
Echoing Saulo’s appeal for prevention efforts to boost resilience among the world’s most vulnerable communities, the UN’s emergency relief chief, Tom Fletcher, described the new El Niño as a “behemoth…a wrecking ball that will likely tear through Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and floods”.
Across Asia and the Pacific, countries must brace for a range of climate shocks, including droughts, floods and cyclones, he said at a news conference.
The global agency also said that some 50 million people could face increased hunger because of the weather phenomenon. It cited the African Development Bank estimate that it would cost African countries between USD 10 and USD 20 billion “and drive down GDP by between one and two per cent”.
“This El Nino will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration. The next two weeks are the critical window to act before that damage is done,” Fletcher added.
The UN Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs proposed “a much wider global mobilisation of solidarity, expertise and action across governments, civil societies, academics, businesses”.
“I am writing to countries with existing disaster response capacity, part of our coordinated emergency network, to ask them to place that capacity on immediate standby to support the effort,” Fletcher said.
India has taken on an international role in weather disaster forecasting and relief in the aftermath. India-UN Development Partnership Fund has sponsored projects for early warning systems, and disaster risk reduction in seven Pacific Island countries.
India along with the other members of the Quad, the US, Japan and Australia, also has Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) programmes for the Indo-Pacific region.
For Southeast Asia, Saulo foresaw “warmer conditions and rainfall deficits increase the risk of heat exposure and place additional pressure on agriculture and water supplies, like the increasing wildfire and smoke hazards risks we are already seeing”.

title: When the Term “Heatwave” Is No Longer Enough - Covering Climate Now
search_term: (heatwave OR "heat wave" OR "severe heatwave" OR "extreme heat" OR "heat spell" OR "scorching heat" OR "blistering heat" OR "sweltering heat" OR "hot winds" OR loo OR "hot loo winds" OR "intense heat" OR "unbearable heat" OR "deadly heat" OR heat OR "weather forecast" OR "weather update" OR "weather alert" OR "IMD forecast" OR "IMD prediction" OR "IMD alert" OR IMD OR "rising temperatures" OR "temperatures expected to rise" OR "relief from heat" OR "respite from heat" OR "heat respite" OR "respite from scorching heat") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
In a landmark piece of climate journalism, Reuters has just published a groundbreaking investigation arguing that the term “heat waves” no longer adequately captures what is happening on the planet. A better term is “heat storms,” wrote Maurice Tamman, a veteran investigative journalist who was the lead reporter on “The Age of Heat Storms” project.
“[S]upersized heatwaves used to be rare,” Tamman wrote. “No longer. Now they swarm the planet.” In a video accompanying the report, he explained that, “whereas heatwaves were once small and relatively self-contained, now we live in a world where these heatwaves are massive.”
Drawing on interviews with dozens of scientists and researchers, Reuters defined a “heat storm” as an episode of “abnormally high temperatures” that lasts for at least five consecutive days and covers more than 1% of Earth’s surface, an area roughly the size of half of Canada. Whereas the planet averaged about five heat storms in the 1960s, the largest of which covered 6% of the planet and lasted for 46 days, the average today is 102 heat storms per year, the largest of which affected 85% of Earth’s surface “and virtually every single human being living in 2023 and 2024.”
Heat storms, Tamman added in the video, are not only larger and stronger than heatwaves, they “are also different in another way: They are cascading, where there is an endless series of storms, one after the other.” Indeed, for the last 18 years straight, “at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one,” according to a fresh analysis of global temperature data that Reuters conducted with the scientists.
Tamman, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 2025 for an exposé of the global fentanyl trade and has covered climate change for years, was drawn to this project after having long been “frustrated by a disconnect between scientists and the public,” he wrote. It can be useful for scientists and policymakers to talk about the need to limit global warming to 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, he acknowledged, but “what is an ordinary person to make of that? Not much.” Extreme heat, on the other hand, is something that ordinary people viscerally understand — and that nearly everyone on Earth has now experienced. In recent months, global warming and the heat that follows has become even more visceral, bringing ever more extreme events like last summer’s Nepal glacier collapse and the deaths of more than 35,000 people across Europe.
Like the best climate reporting, the Reuters investigation both humanized and localized the story. One installment told the story of Justice Trumpler, a 17-year-old high school football captain in Texas who invites college recruiters to watch him play, only to succumb to non-stop vomiting in the 100 degrees Fahrenheit heat and end up in the hospital. Another installment described how hundreds of the iconic pink dolphins that inhabit the Amazon river were literally cooked to death by extreme heat. In the Philippines, a math teacher saw a student face-down on his desk, crying; when the teacher coaxed him to sit up, the boy’s face and chest were covered in blood from a spontaneous nosebleed, a common malady in extreme heat.
All this and more is happening, bear in mind, after average global temperatures have risen by “only” 1.4 degrees C. And because emissions continue to increase, temperatures are projected to rise to at least 1.7 C by roughly 2050, the UN Environment Programme said in its annual “Emissions Gap” report, released yesterday. A key reason emissions keep increasing, The New York Times reported, is that the US under President Donald Trump has reversed the country’s previous efforts to limit fossil fuel production. To limit the amount of “overshoot” of the Paris Agreement goal of 1.5 degrees C of temperature rise, UNEP said, “a massive global scale-up” in emissions reductions will be needed, a goal certain to be discussed at the COP31 UN climate summit taking place in Turkey from November 9 to 20.
To help both the public and policymakers grasp how harshly even today’s 1.4 degrees C of global warming is transforming life on Earth, the Reuters project suggested that heat storms be given names, just as hurricanes routinely are. “Naming events,” the report said, “is ‘a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening,’ Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet ‘we don’t currently do that with heatwaves,’ he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year.”
In online discussions, some meteorologists have bristled at the term “heat storm.” David Dickson, Covering Climate Now’s resident meteorologist, noted that “storm” is a term “with a very distinct meteorological definition that is the opposite of what happens during extreme heat (storms occur with low pressure, heat with high pressure).” However, Dickson added, “I can’t think of a better name, and think it does the job in communicating impacts quite well — and we already have other things described as storms that aren’t, i.e. solar storms.”
For nearly a decade, thousands of climate scientists have been deliberately using the term “emergency” to describe how fast and dangerously global warming is intensifying. Activists picked up the “emergency” framing as well, but the Reuters findings underscore that that framing has always been fundamentally a matter of science, not politics.

Lagos residents spend more to battle intense heat
Intense heat is forcing Lagos residents to spend more on water, electricity and cooling appliances, while others sacrifice sleep and cut household expenses to stay comfortable.
Residents spoke in separate interviews on Thursday in Lagos.
For some, the heat means buying cold drinks more frequently, paying higher electricity bills or seeking alternative sleeping arrangements when their homes become unbearably hot.
In Apongbon Street, Lagos Island, Blessing Olabode said she now spends between N1,100 and N1,300 daily on cold drinks and bottled water, compared with N400 to N900 previously.
“I spend N1,100 to N1,300 every day buying cold drinks and bottled water just to boost my energy, stay hydrated and cool down,” she said.
Ms Olabode’s daily spending could add between N6,000 and N27,000 to her monthly expenses if sustained for 30 days.
She said the heat also disrupted her sleep, leaving her tired the following day and forcing her to cut spending on mobile data and transportation.
Another Apongbon resident, Mercy Favour, said her monthly electricity expenses rose from N10,000 to N15,000 because she used cooling appliances more frequently.
Ms Favour said she bought a rechargeable fan for about N50,000 to help her cope with the heat.
She added that her household’s monthly water expenditure had increased from N48,000 to N60,000 since mid-September.
“The additional water was needed for frequent bathing whenever the electricity supply failed,” she said.
Ms Favour said the heat sometimes woke her four or five times nightly, while alternative cooling equipment, including solar-powered appliances, remained expensive.
Another Apongbon resident, Omolayo Lawal, said rising electricity expenses had forced her to reduce reliance on air conditioning and reconsider other household spending.
Ms Lawal said 20.40 units of electricity, which previously cost N3,000 and lasted a month, now lasted about two weeks.
“I just used money saved for gas to make up for my electricity bill because I don’t want to sleep under this heat,” she said.
For Miss Sandra, who lives on Popoola Street, Mafoluku, the heat has made sleeping inside her apartment almost impossible.
She said she now slept on the decking of her compound at night because her apartment remained unbearably hot.
Ms Sandra, who works with an insurance company, said she also bought cold water almost every hour at work to soak a towel and dab her face and neck.
She attributed her discomfort at home partly to poor electricity supply, which she said was available for barely an hour daily.
“At night, I never sleep inside my apartment. I sleep upstairs on the decking of the compound till daybreak. That is the only way I can get some sleep,” she said.
In Maryland, Ikeja, Eunice Ogbonna said her family had invested in two solar-powered table fans despite owning air conditioners and conventional fans.
She said the larger Sun King solar-powered fan cost about N120,000, while the smaller version sold for approximately N90,000.
Ms Ogbonna said the N210,000 investment provided an alternative during unreliable electricity supply.
“The fans operated for between 12 hours at the highest speed and 19 hours at lower speed settings,” she said.
At Oyingbo Market, a spice vendor, Peculiar Igwe, said her daily spending on chilled bottled water had increased from N400 to about N1,000.
The N600 daily increase could add approximately N18,000 to her monthly expenses if sustained for 30 days.
Ms Igwe said rising fuel costs also made generator use difficult whenever electricity was unavailable, while the heat sometimes forced her to interrupt business activities to rest.
“Fuel that used to last for two days now lasts for only a few hours, increasing the amount we spend to cope with the heat,” she said.
She appealed to the government to reduce fuel prices to make generator use more affordable during electricity shortages.
Meanwhile, Augustina Obioma, a chef on Oshogbo Street, Lawanson, Augustina said she used her fan and air conditioner simultaneously but still struggled with the heat.
Ms Obioma said her monthly electricity expenses had risen from N2,000 to between N4,000 and N5,000 over the past month.
She added that the heat caused discomfort and skin rashes, while her nieces struggled to sleep in the hot conditions.
The Nigerian Institute of Social and Economic Research (NISER) identified extreme heat as an increasingly persistent climate risk in Lagos State in a research brief published on October 8, 2026.
Titled “Managing Heat Risk in Lagos: Protecting Vulnerable Communities from Extreme Heat,: the brief reported heat stress across all study locations, with none recording levels below 35 degrees Celsius.
NISER said high temperatures combined with high humidity intensified heat discomfort, particularly during the dry season.
It also identified heat hotspots in southern Lagos and the city centre.
According to the institute, 75.5 per cent of respondents worked outdoors, increasing their exposure to heat during working hours.
The research also found that 46.3 per cent of households experienced high thermal housing vulnerability, while another 47.2 per cent experienced moderate vulnerability.
NISER reported that 91.3 per cent of households depended on a single income source, potentially limiting their ability to afford additional cooling measures.
The findings highlight the financial pressures facing residents who must contend with intense heat, vulnerable housing and limited access to affordable cooling.
However, the individual accounts do not establish the average additional cost of coping with intense heat across Lagos State.
